cim: AI in 401(k) Retirement Plans: Advice, Admin & Engagement
cim_eredeti: AI in 401(k) Retirement Plans: Advice, Admin & Engagement
szoveg_eredeti:
In this next installment of 401(k) Specialist’s Deep Dive series, we examine the rapid pace of AI technology as it moves from mainstream usage to more specific applications in the workplace retirement plan environment. New semi-autonomous tools are transforming the way that participants learn about their plans and are helping advisors free up their time from complex administrative duties, focusing instead on client needs. But the speed and scale of AI sophistication also raise questions on what parts of the retirement planning experience need more of a human touch.

If it seems like the pace of development and integration of artificial intelligence in nearly every aspect of our lives has moved at an exponential pace, you’re correct. AI-embedded tools automatically pop up to offer sophisticated advice in our word processors, social media and online search tools. In every interaction with the electronic world, it often feels like a decade’s worth of technical progress was made in just the past year alone.

In few areas is that more noticeable than in the world of retirement plan services, where a complex and often old-fashioned system of paper, human experts and complex computations is quickly being infiltrated by AI services. For a participant population that still feels disconnected and confused about saving for retirement (and income in retirement), AI tools can now provide near-human-styled guidance on investments and 401(k) contributions, all from the convenience of a smartphone app.

AI-empowered management platforms are just as quickly rolling out into the retirement plan advisor and plan sponsor worlds, with new systems being developed to electronically coordinate the not-so-well-connected responsibilities of TPAs, recordkeepers, fiduciary and other behind-the-scenes functionalities. Advisors are getting access to a thoroughly modernized range of AI assistants that can drastically simplify the behind-the-scenes scramble of balancing plan documentation, financial recordkeeping and administrative duties, allowing them to spend more time focusing on relationships with their clients.

But the rapid move to a heavily digitized and, in many cases, nearly self-serve approach to retirement planning has many asking if the AI revolution will really serve to help bolster the fortunes of retirement specialists. Or, will the transformative technology will leave advisors feeling like they’ve been left behind, as professionals in many other industries are now seeing their own expertise and personal value outpaced by AI?

Michael Allen, head of Technology, Retirement Solutions with Morningstar Investment Management LLC, has spent the past several years working to help the financial giant keep pace with the increasingly sophisticated money advice that’s already being provided by AI agents on platforms from ChatGPT to Anthropic’s Claude.

“Before trusting any AI tool with client data, I’d ask: Where does my data go? Can it show where an answer came from? And if it makes a recommendation, who stands behind it? If a vendor can’t answer that clearly, that’s your answer.”

“The next wave is personal AI agents,” Allen said. “Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots and Grok Bot are already working in the background on people’s goals, connected to their apps. In retirement, that means an assistant that notices when your life changes and helps you act on it, with your OK. But it only works if real, trusted advice is plugged in.”

According to Evergreen.ai’s Financial Decisions Study, nearly half of Americans asked an AI chatbot about money issues lasts year, with two-thirds of that group made up of people who’d already worked with a financial advisor. Some 80% of those who’d consulted with AI on financial issues subsequently acted on the answers, and almost 30% did so without running the advice by a financial professional or checking it against another source.

Helping steer participants to understanding the value of human expertise in the financial decision-making process will be the next challenge, Allen said, even with the ease and increasing sophistication of AI tools.

“Managed accounts settled whether technology can advise on its own years ago. The real question is who stands behind the advice,” Allen said. “For me, that’s an accountable fiduciary with a methodology you can audit, and AI doesn’t change that.”

Allen said the same standards that apply to every advisor or plan sponsor’s daily responsibilities become even more important as AI becomes more prevalent.

“Before trusting any AI tool with client data, I’d ask: Where does my data go? Can it show where an answer came from? And if it makes a recommendation, who stands behind it? If a vendor can’t answer that clearly, that’s your answer,” Allen said.

For advisors, the AI learning curve begins as they work to better integrate the growing range of specialized, industry-specific AI productivity tools into their own workflow. The more difficult part will be demonstrating the value of their personal expertise as more and more workers use readily accessible AI tools to begin making financial plans on their own, or to get a digital second opinion.

That heavy consumer lean-in on AI resources and financial insight is a significant challenge for retirement professionals, who may see their prized skillset of technical knowledge—and their livelihoods—threatened by easily accessible online tools.

Noted financial services marketing consultant Sheri Fitts describes herself as the ultimate early adopter of AI technology, and an advocate for understanding the realities of AI’s impact on retirement professionals.

“In every case, the technology is doing the heavy lifting on the complicated stuff. But the human is still the one making meaning. Still the one reading the room. Still the one deciding what matters.”

“About a year and half prior to Chat GPT launching in November 2022, I was using an early AI tool that’s now called Jasper… but it felt really weird. I was using it to get better subject lines for my emails, and I felt like I was cheating. Over time, I got more and more comfortable with the platform, but the voice was still way off.”

Fitts said the debut of ChatGPT was a revolutionary transition point, as it introduced the world to an AI product that nearly everybody could use. Now, as she bounces between Muse, Claude and ChatGPT on a daily basis, she compares the anxiety around AI’s rollout to the compliance concerns that emerged during the pandemic when advisors had to exclusively use Zoom calls for client meetings, practically overnight. AI’s near-magic capabilities can be a lot to deal with, even for personal tasks.

“A lot of people ask me, ‘so, who’s looking at this?’ And I’m trying to explain that there’s no one looking at this. This is ones and zeros, really. It started as a predictive machine, which you saw happening in your emails, as it tried to guess what you were saying and complete a sentence for you,” Fitts said.

Rather than fighting the AI revolution, Fitts said it’s time to claim it as a productivity tool. In a report created for SWAY, her branding program for financial professionals, Fitts said she encourages advisors to consider AI as the ultimate copilot to personal success, as she feels the technology has not yet transformed the financial services world quite as broadly as some suggest.

Fitts cites Edelman research that said that only 32% of Americans currently trust AI, and Deloitte numbers showing that just 11% of lower-revenue financial services firms have reported measurable ROI from their AI investments. AI itself, she noted, does not create clarity; it simply exposes whether clarity even exists.

Instead of worrying about it taking your job away, Fitts suggests retirement professionals use AI’s growth as opportunity to refine the values they bring to the industry: knowledge, personal service, integrity and trust.
